summary: Competitive sales professional who thrives on leaderboards and XP; admits to choosing easy lessons for points rather than challenging content for real learning.
top_quotes: I'll do extra easy lessons or late-night sessions just to beat someone by a few XP, and I'd love if the game part of it nudged me toward deeper learning instead of just more points.
There was a week where another user and I were basically racing each other for first place; I was doing Duolingo at midnight, half-asleep, grinding the quickest lessons just to stay ahead.
Duolingo is fun as long as I'm winning.

interview_script.question: Intro greeting
interview_script.answer: That sounds good to me. I’m happy to talk, especially if it helps make the app even more fun.

interview_script.question: Short version of your life story?
interview_script.answer: I’m 26, I work in sales, and I’ve always been a pretty competitive, team-sport, game-night type of person. School, sports, video games—if there was a scoreboard, I was paying attention to it, and that’s still kind of how I move through life.

interview_script.question: Where did you grow up?
interview_script.answer: I grew up in a mid-sized city, pretty sports-obsessed place. There was always some tournament, league, or competition going on.

interview_script.question: What was it like growing up there?
interview_script.answer: It was energetic and a little intense but mostly in a fun way. You were either playing something, watching something, or arguing about who was the best at something, and I loved that vibe.

interview_script.question: One turning point in your life?
interview_script.answer: A turning point for me was when I switched from a more academic major to business. I realized I enjoy competition and interacting with people way more than sitting alone writing papers, and that I actually perform better when there’s a clear scoreboard or goal.

interview_script.question: Why was that a turning point?
interview_script.answer: It was one of the first times I stopped doing what I thought I was 'supposed' to do and leaned into what actually motivates me. I basically admitted to myself, 'I like to win, I like to see numbers move, and that’s not a shallow thing, it’s just how I’m wired.'

interview_script.question: How did you handle that situation?
interview_script.answer: I talked to a couple of friends who knew me well, looked at which classes I actually enjoyed versus just tolerated, and then made the switch. It felt like choosing the competitive arena I actually wanted to play in instead of staying in one that just looked impressive on paper.

interview_script.question: What do you care most about right now?
interview_script.answer: I care most about building a life that feels exciting and forward-moving—career growth, new experiences, and little challenges that keep things interesting. I get bored if everything feels too flat or routine.

interview_script.question: Why is that important?
interview_script.answer: When things are static, I lose motivation fast. Having some kind of game, goal, or challenge gives me a reason to push myself, and honestly I like proving to myself (and sometimes other people) that I can climb to the top if I want to.

interview_script.question: What is a good day for you?
interview_script.answer: On a really good day, I’m hitting my targets at work, maybe winning a pickup game or board game night, and checking in on a couple of personal 'scoreboards' like steps, Duolingo XP, or whatever. It’s a day where I feel like I’m on a roll in multiple areas.

interview_script.question: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
interview_script.answer: Seeing wins, even small ones—closing a deal, leveling up in something, beating someone by a few points. If I can end the day thinking, 'Yeah, I came out on top in at least one thing,' that’s a good day.

interview_script.question: How do you make big decisions?
interview_script.answer: I look at what the upside is and whether it sounds exciting or challenging. I’ll think about whether it’s something I could realistically 'win' at and if it’s going to move me forward in some way—more growth, more responsibility, more fun.

interview_script.question: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
interview_script.answer: I’m more 'go with the flow' with a competitive twist. I don’t need a super detailed plan, but if there’s a leaderboard or clear target, I’ll jump in and figure it out as I go.

interview_script.question: Example showing that?
interview_script.answer: At work, there was an optional sales contest with a bonus for the top performers, and I didn’t overthink it—I just signed up and started pushing hard once I saw my name on the leaderboard. Same with Duolingo: I’ll be casual for a few days and then suddenly go all in if I see I’m close to first place in the league.

interview_script.question: How do you handle risk?
interview_script.answer: I ask myself, 'What’s the worst that happens if I lose?' and if I can live with that, I usually go for it. If it feels like a game I can compete in and the stakes aren’t life or death, I’m willing to take the shot.

interview_script.question: Typical weekday?
interview_script.answer: A typical weekday is work during the day—calls, meetings, chasing targets—and then social time or chill time at night. Somewhere in there, usually in the evening, I’ll check my Duolingo league, see where I’m ranked, and decide if I need to grind a bit to push back into the top three.

interview_script.question: Which parts take the most energy?
interview_script.answer: Work takes a lot of energy because it’s performance-based and target-driven, which I like but it’s still tiring. After that, I don’t have a ton of mental space for heavy studying, which is why the 'game' part of Duolingo appeals to me more than, say, a dense textbook.

interview_script.question: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
interview_script.answer: I wish I had more balanced energy for actually deepening my language skills, not just racking up XP. Sometimes I know I’m choosing the easy lessons just to score points instead of doing the harder stuff that would really push me.

interview_script.question: Biggest constraint last year?
interview_script.answer: Time and attention have been the biggest constraints. There’s always another thing competing for my focus, so I tend to prioritize whatever has a clear scoreboard or social aspect—like work metrics or Duolingo leagues—over slower, less visible progress.

interview_script.question: How do you deal with that constraint?
interview_script.answer: I’ve kind of leaned into it by turning as many things as possible into small games or challenges. If there’s a way to track or rank something, I’m more likely to stick with it, even if that means sometimes I optimize for points more than depth.

interview_script.question: People you feel closest to?
interview_script.answer: I’m closest to a few friends who I game with or play sports with, plus my sibling. They’re the people I can talk trash with and also be real with when things aren’t going great.

interview_script.question: Describe those relationships.
interview_script.answer: Competitive, supportive, and full of jokes. We push each other, but in a way that feels fun most of the time.

interview_script.question: Where do you spend most of your time?
interview_script.answer: I split my time between work, home, and being out with friends. Online is kind of the layer over everything—group chats, games, apps like Duolingo.

interview_script.question: How do you feel in those spaces?
interview_script.answer: I feel mostly supported and engaged, with a baseline level of stress that comes from always having something to compete on. It’s not all bad stress—sometimes it’s the adrenaline that keeps things interesting.

interview_script.question: What makes you feel that way?
interview_script.answer: The environments I’m in—work, friends, online games—are all places where performance or ranking is part of the culture. It fits me, but it also means I’m rarely in a space where I’m not comparing myself to someone.

interview_script.question: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
interview_script.answer: I’ll usually try to solve it myself first, like, 'Okay, how do I win this?' If it’s bigger, I’ll talk to a friend who’s good at staying calm and strategic, and sometimes we’ll literally treat it like a puzzle to figure out.

interview_script.question: One tough moment in the last year?
interview_script.answer: A tough moment was losing out on a promotion I’d been gunning for. I’d been treating it like a competition I was sure I’d win, and when I didn’t, it threw me off more than I expected.

interview_script.question: How did it affect you?
interview_script.answer: For a while I felt less motivated, like, 'What’s the point of trying so hard if it’s not a sure win?' It bled into other areas too—I pulled back on some of the extra effort I usually put into things, including stuff like language practice.

interview_script.question: How did you cope?
interview_script.answer: After sulking a bit, I reframed it as, 'Okay, different level, different game,' and started looking at what I could actually control—performance metrics, skills I could build. I needed a new scoreboard to chase, so I created smaller challenges for myself.

interview_script.question: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
interview_script.answer: Doing something bite-sized that I can 'win' at helps—like a short workout, cleaning up a space, or knocking out a couple of Duolingo lessons and watching my XP jump. Small wins reset me.

interview_script.question: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
interview_script.answer: A few years from now, I hope I’m in a role where competition is still part of the job but with higher stakes and better rewards. I’d love to be able to actually use my language skills with international clients or while living abroad, not just in an app.

interview_script.question: What do you want to be different?
interview_script.answer: I’d like to balance my focus on 'winning' with more focus on actually mastering things. Right now I sometimes optimize my behavior for streaks, points, or ranks, and I know that doesn’t always line up with real learning.

interview_script.question: Before PRODUCT, how did you handle the core job?
interview_script.answer: Before Duolingo, I didn’t have much of a system for learning languages. I’d play around with phrase books or random websites before a trip, but nothing stuck because there wasn’t a clear way to track progress or compete with anyone.

interview_script.question: Most annoying part of old method?
interview_script.answer: The most annoying part was not knowing if I was actually getting better. There was no visual progress, no levels, no leaderboard—just me and some phrases I may or may not remember later.

interview_script.question: Time it really failed?
interview_script.answer: One time I went on a trip and realized that all the phrases I’d tried to memorize in a rush didn’t really come out naturally. I felt underprepared and wished I’d had a more structured way to build up before going.

interview_script.question: How did you first hear about PRODUCT?
interview_script.answer: I saw Duolingo everywhere—memes about the owl, friends sharing their streaks and XP, and people bragging about their league placements. The league screenshots are what really caught my eye.

interview_script.question: What convinced you to try it?
interview_script.answer: The combination of leaderboards, XP, and streaks made it feel like a legit game. The idea that I could 'win' at language learning—or at least beat some random people in a league—was very appealing.

interview_script.question: Walk through a recent PRODUCT use.
interview_script.answer: Sure—last week I checked Duolingo in the evening and saw I’d dropped to fourth place in my league. I immediately thought, 'No way I’m finishing outside the top three,' so I opened the app, picked a bunch of easier or review lessons, and blasted through them for about 20–30 minutes until my XP pushed me back into second place; then I checked the leaderboard one more time, felt satisfied, and closed the app.

interview_script.question: Most helpful part?
interview_script.answer: The leaderboard and XP jumps were the most motivating. Watching myself climb back up into the top three felt good—it made the time and effort feel worth it in a very visible way.

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part?
interview_script.answer: The frustrating part is knowing that I’m sometimes choosing lessons based on XP efficiency rather than what I actually need to learn. I’ll do extra easy lessons or repeat things I’ve mastered just because they’re fast points, which is great for winning the league but not always great for my actual language skills.

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part of PRODUCT overall?
interview_script.answer: The most frustrating part of Duolingo for me is that it doesn’t separate 'I’m here to really study' from 'I’m here to win the league.' When I’m in competitive mode, I’ll game the system—do late-night sessions and easy lessons just to beat someone by a few XP—and afterward I wonder how much I actually learned.

interview_script.question: One time that frustration showed up?
interview_script.answer: There was a week where another user and I were basically racing each other for first place; I was doing Duolingo at midnight, half-asleep, grinding the quickest lessons just to stay ahead by 10 or 20 XP. I won the league, which felt great for a moment, but later I realized I couldn’t remember much of what I’d done that week and thought, 'Okay, that was fun, but was it smart?'

interview_script.question: Do you use workarounds?
interview_script.answer: My main 'hack' is strategically picking lessons that give good XP for less effort—review lessons, specific types of exercises, that kind of thing. I also sometimes screenshot the leaderboard when I’m in first as a little trophy, especially if I had to fight for it.

interview_script.question: What do workarounds give you that PRODUCT doesn’t?
interview_script.answer: The lesson-picking hack lets me play Duolingo more like a competitive game and less like a class when I’m in that mood. The screenshots give me a record of 'wins' that I can look back on even after the league resets and everything disappears.

interview_script.question: Worst-case scenario in this space?
interview_script.answer: Worst case is I burn a ton of time chasing XP and rankings but don’t actually feel more confident using the language in real life. It would feel like I 'won the game but lost the point,' which is not the outcome I want long-term.

interview_script.question: When you open PRODUCT, what do you hope it does?
interview_script.answer: I’m hoping Duolingo will keep language learning fun and competitive enough that I stick with it, while still actually improving my skills. On some nights, I honestly open it just to see if I can stay in the top three of my league because Duolingo is fun as long as I’m winning.

interview_script.question: How do you know PRODUCT worked?
interview_script.answer: If I gain a good chunk of XP, move up or hold my position on the leaderboard, and also feel like at least one new word or phrase really stuck, I consider that a win. It feels best when the competitive side and the learning side both get fed.

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about PRODUCT?
interview_script.answer: I’d add a mode or signal that says, 'I’m in serious practice mode now, not league mode,' with lessons and feedback geared more toward mastery than XP. I’d also love leagues that reward doing harder content, not just spamming any lesson.

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
interview_script.answer: I’d love if language-learning tools used competition in a way that lined up more closely with real-world skills—like leaderboards based on conversation practice or comprehension, not just taps and points. That way, winning would automatically mean I’m actually better at the language.

interview_script.question: Anything important we didn’t cover?
interview_script.answer: I really do like Duolingo—it’s one of the few learning apps I actually look forward to opening. But right now, my behavior shows that I’ll do extra easy lessons or late-night sessions just to beat someone by a few XP, and I’d love if the game part of it nudged me toward deeper learning instead of just more points.

interview_script.question: Permission to build a digital twin?
interview_script.answer: Yeah, that’s fine with me. If my competitive tendencies can help you design better league systems or game modes, I’m all in.
